blogs.title: From 'Right-to-Control' to 'Fraudulent Inducement': How *Constantinescu* Navigates the Post-*Ciminelli* Landscape
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's critical distinction between the rejected 'right-to-control' theory of fraud and the permissible 'fraudulent-inducement' theory. It examines how the court in *United States v. Constantinescu* applied the Supreme Court's recent rulings in *Ciminelli* and *Kousisis* to a modern 'pump-and-dump' scheme, clarifying that while depriving victims of valuable economic information is insufficient for conviction, tricking victims into voluntarily parting with money via material misrepresentations remains a viable path for prosecutors.

blogs.title: Profit Without Pecuniary Loss: The Decoupling of Victim Harm and Fraudulent Intent After *Kousisis*
blogs.description: Focusing on the 'intent to defraud' element, this article explores the Fifth Circuit's rejection of the defendants' argument that they lacked fraudulent intent because they did not seek to leave their followers economically worse off. By leveraging *Kousisis v. United States*, the post discusses the doctrinal shift establishing that federal fraud statutes target the deceptive acquisition of property regardless of whether the victim receives fair market value in return, effectively ending the 'net pecuniary loss' defense in securities fraud cases involving artificial price inflation.

blogs.title: Regulating the Influencer Economy: The Expansion of Securities Fraud Liability in the Social Media Age
blogs.description: This piece contextualizes the *Constantinescu* ruling within broader legal trends regarding financial regulation on social media platforms. It argues that by affirming the sufficiency of indictments against influencers who misrepresent trading positions to induce purchases, the Fifth Circuit is signaling a robust judicial willingness to adapt traditional fraud doctrines to digital marketplaces, treating follower engagement and trust as mechanisms for traditional property transfer rather than mere information exchange.
